source.title: Deep learning generalizes because the parameter-function map is biased towards simple functions
source.authors: Guillermo Valle Pérez; Chico Q. Camargo; A. Louis

record.tranche_reason: The study trains networks on natural and increasingly corrupted labels and reports held-out error, testing whether natural-label generalization coexists with fitting corrupted labels. It does not reproduce Zhang et al.'s exact architectures or setup.
record.gate_note: The study states that training error is 0 in all Figure 3 experiments and that the Boolean network can fit random functions. Figure 3 reports generalization error across label-corruption levels; the Boolean-function experiments also report generalization error versus target complexity. PAC-Bayes bounds and simplicity-bias measurements do not directly measure the versioned behavior and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures zero-training-error fitting and held-out error as image labels are corrupted, extending V1 to binary classification on three datasets. Its CNN–fully connected comparisons also test V3.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors propose simplicity bias in the parameter-function map as a main explanation for generalization and report empirical support and comparatively tight function-space PAC-Bayes bounds. They emphasize that the SGD sampling assumption and other approximations require further validation, and that their account does not yet explain practical training tricks.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SGD and zero training error on binarized datasets with CNN and fully connected architectures; tests label-corruption trends rather than reproducing Zhang et al.'s exact experiment. It also studies parameter-to-function probabilities and PAC-Bayes bounds.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and architecture change the reported zero-corruption generalization error; the bound's relationship to dataset difficulty also depends on variance hyperparameters, as described in Appendix C.

fits_no_version.finding: Random parameter sampling strongly favors simple functions, and function-space PAC-Bayes bounds follow several empirical error trends.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The parameter-function map induces a simplicity-biased prior that can help explain generalization, subject to the sampling and approximation assumptions.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic Boolean tasks, generalization worsens with target complexity; truly random targets yield error equal to or above an unbiased learner.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expressive Boolean networks generalize better on structured targets than on random targets; this is distinct from V1's natural-image-label comparison.

record.problems: The central SGD sampling assumption is described as informal and needing further work. The study notes that the choice of Gaussian weight and bias variances affects the bounds; measured trained-weight variances yielded significantly worse bounds. Figure 3 reports empirical errors averaged over 8 initializations, but Table 1 provides no uncertainty values.

untested.parts: The specified original architectures and multiclass CIFAR-10/ImageNet experiments are not reproduced. Exact chance-level held-out performance at full randomization cannot be verified from the supplied figure extraction.
No width sweep measuring test error beyond the interpolation threshold.
No isolation of local connectivity, learned sparse connections, or initialization from a trained CNN; no CIFAR-100 or SVHN comparison. The tested architectures also differ in depth.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison of held-out performance under the specified tuning conditions.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No dropout intervention measuring held-out error.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or ranking against generalization gaps.
No removal and retraining comparison using memorization-ranked versus random examples.

missing.what: Separate corruption endpoints for each architecture and dataset, recording the randomization procedure, maximum corruption level, zero training error and corresponding held-out error. The trend rows do not establish the chance-level endpoint.
Explicit paired CNN–FC error comparisons. Existing R1–R6 contain the values but omit their connection to V3.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. R1–R6 each measure one component of V1; the coexistence interpretation additionally relies on the corruption experiments. Increasing error with corruption alone does not establish chance performance on fully random labels. For R3–R4, the shared state field records the V1 result; their V3 assessment is stated separately in the problem fields.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the specified Inception, AlexNet, MLP, or ImageNet cases; does not use the exact Zhang et al. 2017 setup. The Boolean-function learning experiment is not the same as the specified CIFAR-10 random-label comparison.

relationships.condition: Natural-label binary MNIST, fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 classification with CNN and FC architectures also trained under label corruption
relationships.reason: R1–R6 report zero training error with held-out errors 0.023–0.341, below the 0.5 chance baseline; Section 6 separately describes zero-error fitting under corruption and high-corruption memorization. This supports coexistence, while the exact random-label endpoint remains unreadable.
relationships.display_finding: Natural-label training error was zero and held-out errors were 0.023–0.341 against 0.5 chance, alongside zero-error corrupted-label fitting without a recoverable fully random-label test endpoint.
